messages:
neil: quick q — if we introduce a 'cleanroom' handoff boundary between the admission queue and the coalescer, are we implicitly serializing tenants?
anya: not necessarily. idea is a lightweight contract: queue A produces batches marked safe-to-run, queue B consumes. no global lock, just a handoff token.
sam: main risk i see is double-copying requests during handoff -> mem + latency. can we hand off by pointer/ref instead of copying body?
neil: pointer handoff works, but lifecycle tokens are required so GC/eviction doesn't free the buffer mid-run. we need refcounts or epoch-based GC.
maria: also, observability suffers if batches become opaque across boundaries. we should emit small events: batch.boundary.handoff {id, origin_ts, tenant, sample_keys} so traces stitch.
anya: agreed — keep per-request meta tiny. propose header like `X-Batch-Handoff: id=abc123;origin=1748754321` (proto-compatible). doesn't mutate payload.
infra-bot: deploy: feature-flag batch-handoff-pointer toggle -> staging :rocket:
sam: ran microbench w/ pointer handoff opt-in: -3ms p50, but saw ~12% p99 regressions tied to transient GC spikes on staging.
neil: that matches the tradeoff: median latency down, tail risk up. do we accept tail regression for median wins?
maria: leaning no for SLA-bound tenants. for best-effort workloads ok. maybe make pointer-handoff opt-in per-tenant and default to copy-handoff for production tenants.
anya: another option: 3-way handshake (reserve->fill->commit). slightly more chattiness but simplifies tracing and avoids double-commit races. deterministic GC semantics too.
sam: handshake also buys us clearer backpressure signals — queue A can refuse reserve if it detects high headroom pressure.
neil: action: prototype handshake sketch in adapter layer next sprint, toggle pointer-handoff as an experiment in staging. add batch.boundary events to the tracing schema.
maria: i'll draft a short RFC addendum: lifecycle tokens, tracing events, and per-tenant opt-in policy. will ping y'all for review. :memo: 
anya: thanks — tagging @sam for perf notes and @neil for GC/allocator concerns.
neil: ack.
